Mr Murali Pillai
Long-term national plans

Several plans, including defence transformation, net zero, aviation, maritime, transport, infrastructure and innovation, will take decades to complete.

  2. s00003Mr Murali Pillai — Bukit Batok

    A good number of these plans, especially the ones dealing with the transformation of our defence capabilities, implementing our net zero ambition, developing our sustainable aviation and maritime hubs, transport systems and infrastructural capabilities and building an innovation economy will take decades to complete.

      Just one year ago, if you said software could generate photo-realistic images of scenes and events which never happened just through some text instructions written and keyed in via a keyboard, you might have been told that was some way off.

    2. s01385Dr Tan Wu Meng — Jurong

      And yet, today, we have ChatGPT, GPT-4 architecture, Midjourney 5 – and that is just one year on.

    • Dr Tan Wu Meng
    AI challenges for social trust

    States that AI will pose great challenges for social togetherness and social trust.

    1. s01404Dr Tan Wu Meng — Jurong

      AI will pose great challenges for social togetherness and social trust.

    • Dr Tan Wu Meng
    Foreign troublemakers using deepfakes

    Foreign troublemakers may try to damage society by circulating deepfakes of community incidents and opinion shapers.

    1. s01408Dr Tan Wu Meng — Jurong

      You can imagine how foreign troublemakers will try to damage our society – circulating deepfakes of community incidents that never happened, deepfakes of opinion shapers or people in the news.

    • Dr Tan Wu Meng
    Social cohesion under AI disruption

    Policymakers not thinking about strengthening social cohesion will see business-as-usual policies weaken social togetherness in an AI-disrupted world.

    1. s01412Dr Tan Wu Meng — Jurong

      If you are a policymaker and you are not already thinking about how to strengthen social cohesion in this brave new world, then business-as-usual policies will actually mean the progressive weakening of our social togetherness in a world disrupted by AI and generative AI.

    • Dr Tan Wu Meng
    Neighbourhood centres and hawker centres

    It asks whether policymakers favour more hawker centres and coffee shops to bring people together, or let the market decide.

    1. s01420Dr Tan Wu Meng — Jurong

      When neighbourhood centres are designed and outfitted, do policymakers lean in favour of having more hawker centres and coffee shops as a way of bringing people together, even building, designing ahead of demand, or does the market get to decide after the fact?

    • Dr Tan Wu Meng
    AI customising student learning

    AI can customise learning to each student's skills, but this does not mean teachers will become obsolete.

    1. s01456Dr Tan Wu Meng — Jurong

      With AI, it will be possible to customise the learning process to each student's individual skills, understanding what works best for that particular student.

    2. s01457Dr Tan Wu Meng — Jurong

      This does not mean teachers will become obsolete.

    • Dr Tan Wu Meng
    Human relationships amid AI disruption

    It calls for public policy to bring Singaporeans together for face-to-face interactions, strengthening human relationships and trust amid AI disruption.

    1. s01460Dr Tan Wu Meng — Jurongcontext

      It means educators could have more time to befriend students, understand each student's journey, be that cheerleader, that mentor, that shoulder to cry on in times of difficulty, or that person to motivate the student to grow beyond what they dreamed they could do.

    2. s01461Dr Tan Wu Meng — Jurong

      We need to make sure our Public Service deeply understands AI and its opportunities, whether in health, whether in defence, but across the board in policymaking.

    3. s01462Dr Tan Wu Meng — Jurongcontext

      Amid a world of AIs, deep fakes and generative AI creations, we need to double down in our public policy on how we bring people together, on how we bring fellow Singaporeans together for these face-to-face interactions, which will be the key bedrock foundation of our society and inoculation against deep fakes and other AI disruptions.

    4. s01463Dr Tan Wu Meng — Jurong

      We need to strengthen human relationships, deepen human trust and we need policy to guide that direction in a world of AI disruption, so that amid big changes in the world, Singapore and Singaporeans continue having that sense of togetherness so that we can survive and thrive in a dangerous world and continue to dream and overcome whatever the world throws at us.

    1. s01493Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo — East Coast

    2. s01500Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo — East Coast

      Means-testing qualifying criteria for caregiving support for middle-income Singaporeans may work against some middle-income families that care for their family members.

    Review eldercare support qualifying criteria

    3. s01521Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo — East Coast

      I appeal for a review of the criteria to qualify for support for eldercare services, intermediate and long-term, to better support families as they care for their loved ones.

    The speaker says they are still awaiting the anti-discrimination legislation announced by the Prime Minister nearly two years ago.

    1. s01565Ms Sylvia Lim — Aljunied

    Lowering voting age to 18

    The speaker believes the voting age should be lowered from 21 to 18, noting Singapore is among a handful of countries that has not done so.

      Nevertheless, I believe one change that should be made is to give younger cohorts a direct say in our national elections by lowering the voting age from 21 to 18 years.

    2. s01592Ms Sylvia Lim — Aljuniedcontext

    3. s01593Ms Sylvia Lim — Aljunied

    • Mr Christopher de Souza
    Suggested anti-scam solutions

    The speaker suggests solutions including transaction limits, phone calls to account owners, spotting suspicious patterns in consecutive transactions, and a bank-activated kill switch.

    2. s01642Mr Christopher de Souza — Holland-Bukit Timah

      But that is out of 31,728 scams just in 2022 and over $660 million were reported to have been stolen.

    4. s01654Mr Christopher de Souza — Holland-Bukit Timah

      For many of the elderly who are scammed, the loss is often at least six figures, which is close to their entire retirement savings.

    Parliamentary questions and motions

    • Mr Chan Chun Sing
    Definition of social compact

    A social compact is responsibilities towards one another, how work is rewarded, fruits distributed, and how people relate to and respect one another.

    1. s02288Mr Chan Chun Sing

      A social compact, is simply our responsibilities towards one another, how we reward work and distribute the fruits of labour and success, and how we relate to and respect one another.

    • Mr Chan Chun Sing
    Meritocracy and evolving metrics

    Singapore's relevance depends on evolving, so meritocracy based on a single static metric cannot build a resilient society with diverse strengths.

    1. s02311Mr Chan Chun Singcontext

      Indeed, our relevance and competitiveness as a country depend on our ability to evolve with the times.

    2. s02312Mr Chan Chun Sing

      Hence, meritocracy based on any single, static and narrow metric for talent and ability, will not allow us to build a resilient society with a diversity of strengths to meet tomorrow's challenges.

    • Mr Chan Chun Sing
    Continuous meritocracy system

    Society must have continuous meritocracy where no single test or point in time determines the rest of one's life.

    1. s02318Mr Chan Chun Sing

      For society to allow everyone to do justice to their gifts, we must have a system of continuous meritocracy where no single test or point in time determines the rest of one's life.

    • Mr Chan Chun Sing
    Wealth and privilege transfer

    Access to opportunities and rewards could increasingly be determined by transfer of wealth and privileges from previous generations.

    1. s02326Mr Chan Chun Sing

      Access to opportunities and rewards could increasingly be determined not just by the merits of this generation, but the transfer of wealth and privileges from the previous generations.

    • Mr Chan Chun Sing
    Six strategies for meritocracy

    Government and people will focus on six strategies, moving away from single metrics, with Full SBB making education more flexible.

    1. s02330Mr Chan Chun Singcontext

      To keep our Singaporean meritocracy resilient and sustainable, this Government, together with our people, will focus on six key strategies.

    2. s02331Mr Chan Chun Sing

      We will continue to move away from evaluating our people's diverse abilities by any single, static and narrow metric – be it the PSLE results, grade-point averages or whether they hold a degree or diploma.

    3. s02332Mr Chan Chun Sing

      With the implementation of Full SBB next year, our education system will become more flexible and provide multiple pathways to cater to different learner profiles.

    1. s02355Mr Chan Chun Sing

      Our publicly-funded university degrees will also have a higher lifetime cohort participation rate so that more Singaporeans can look forward to obtaining a degree from our autonomous universities – not necessarily before starting work but at some point in their working lives.

    • Mr Chan Chun Sing
    Solidarity, responsibility and lifelong upskilling

    The passage calls for strengthening solidarity and collective assurance while preserving individual responsibility and agency, and for helping everyone upskill and give back.

    • Mr Chan Chun Sing · Mr Don Wee
    Success for next generation and meritocracy

    The passage states success includes enabling the next generation to be more successful and building a resilient meritocratic society, and notes one in 150 children in Singapore has autism.

    1. s02435Mr Chan Chun Sing

      The mark of our success is not just how well we enable this generation to achieve success, but how well we establish the conditions for the next generation to be even more successful than us.

    2. s02436Mr Chan Chun Singcontext

      Only so will we be able to continuously write new chapters of the Singapore Story.

    3. s02437Mr Chan Chun Sing

      There may never be a perfect system to develop all the perfect students or workers for our societal needs.

    4. s02438Mr Chan Chun Sing

      But, we can all contribute our part to build a better or less imperfect system to continually inspire our people and all who believe in our dream to build a resilient and sustainable meritocratic system to bring out the best from all – to be a beacon of cohesion with unity of purpose in a troubled world; a society with a sense of collective responsibility towards one another; a society with respect for diverse abilities; a society that rewards hard work and talent; a society that recognises contributions beyond achievements; a society with gratitude for our blessings to want to do good for all beyond ourselves.

    5. s02439Mr Chan Chun Sing

      And finally, a nation confident to defy the odds of history to survive and thrive beyond SG100.

    • Ms Hany Soh
    Reviewing Mental Capacity Act

    A suggestion was made for the Government to review the Mental Capacity Act so certain next-of-kin can be default deputies.

    1. s03955Ms Hany Soh — Marsiling-Yew Tee

    2. s03956Ms Hany Soh — Marsiling-Yew Tee

    3. s03957Ms Hany Soh — Marsiling-Yew Tee
